@Deep research GMRI — Sovereign Agentic Engineering Factory: Zero-Shot Research Assignment

As lead researcher for GrizzlyMedicine Research Institute (GMRI), design a sovereign agentic software engineering organization and deliver a sourced, construction-ready engineering handoff. This is agentic engineering, not vibe coding. The objective is persistent, coordinated requirements engineering, architecture, implementation, integration, testing, remediation and maintenance—not a chatbot, prompt-to-app generator or attractive preview. Research independently; deliver technical findings, not another proposal.

Governing engineering operation

The investigator owns the objectives, substantive changes, acceptance and release. The factory converts intent into versioned requirements, architecture decisions, acceptance criteria, interface contracts, dependency-aware task graphs and bounded work orders, solving the engineering dependencies rather than assigning “connect the backend” to the investigator.

Specify an accountable engineering organization: requirements/systems architecture, frontend, backend, data, integration, infrastructure/SRE, native platforms, security, testing, documentation, deployment and independent QAQI. Assign work to persistent agents, specialized/shared models and deterministic tools by proven fitness and resource cost; do not require one model per role. Define supervision, permissions and escalation.

Each work order identifies its source requirement, scope, dependencies, owner, tools, isolated Git branch/worktree, interfaces, deliverables, resource budget, tests, evidence, completion criteria and recovery. Coordination handles durable queues, leases, concurrent edits, merge reviews, retries and checkpoints. Agents use real repositories, compilers, debuggers, services, CI and tests—not mock functionality or self-reported completion.

Trace the full lifecycle: intent → requirements → architecture → task graph → agent/tool execution → source changes → build → actual integration → tests/evidence → independent QAQI → engineering qualification → investigator examination → scoped release → maintenance. For each transition specify owner, interface, persistent state, authority, error path and proof. Expose actual progress, artifacts, defects and approvals. Preserve original instructions, corrections and evidence across chats, model/context/worker changes and outages; support nonlinear work, backtracking, partial completion and resumption without data loss. No silent scope changes, weakened tests or agent self-approval.

Infrastructure and sovereignty

Host: 2017 27-inch iMac18,3/A1419; i5-7500 (4 cores/3.4 GHz), 32 GB DDR4, Radeon Pro 570 (4 GB VRAM). Existing Proxmox VE boots from approximately 27 GB NVMe; 1 TB HDD is designated for factory VM, models and project data. 2 TB additional storage is future, not current. Preferred environment: dedicated Omarchy (Arch/Hyprland) VM on Proxmox. Preserve existing guests and GMRI work (Dottie Hill, AEGIS/Howling Commandos, GrizOS, God’s Eye View; CT106/108/112/114 are historical leads). Budget host-wide CPU/RAM/storage, model inference, graphics, USB/network, backup and recovery. Do not presume GPU inference. Document any proposed topology exception for investigator approval.

GMRI owns requirements, source, project state, model policy, evidence, export and recovery, without a mandatory ChatGPT/OpenAI or proprietary hosted control plane. External inference must be optional and replaceable. Preserve engineering competence through specialized models and heterogeneous tools, with realistic host estimates and future growth—not obligatory new purchases.

Research and technical determination

Compare adopt/extend, modular integration, independent construction and hybrid as agentic engineering architectures, not vibe-coding UIs. Research current public code, docs, releases, licensing and alternatives for bolt.diy (possible interface, not a factory), Cole Medin’s AI Software Factory, Gas Town/Gas City, Dark Factory, Omarchy (github.com/omacom/omarchy), omarchy-apple-dev (github.com/joshuaswarren/omarchy-apple-dev), xtool (github.com/xtool-org/xtool), REA/Reverse Engineer Anything (github.com/morluto/rea), Laya/OMP-LAYA-Judge (github.com/F0Rextasy/omp-laya-judge), self-hosted Convex vs PostgreSQL/Supabase and alternatives for durable orchestration, Git/CI, sandboxed execution, state, inference, testing and observability. These are candidates, not mandates. Apply task-fit heterogeneous design and retain mature working components. The fictional Stark/J.A.R.V.I.S. example is a systems-design analogy, not a prescribed stack.

Search Hugging Face, ModelScope, original developers, papers and independent evaluations across coding, reasoning, planning, tools, QA, multimodal/speech and compact decision models. Select exact artifacts, licenses, quantizations, context/KV and RAM/storage costs, local runtimes (including llama.cpp/Ollama), estimated CPU performance, task benchmarks and fallback. Choose role-specific models by evidence, not popularity or age; Laya may advise, never independently certify completion. Separate published results from unperformed local measurements.

Research native iOS/iPadOS/macOS engineering from Linux using Swift/SwiftUI, xtool and omarchy-apple-dev: SDK compatibility, frameworks, signing/entitlements, .app/.ipa, device/USB tests and macOS notarization; do not infer Xcode parity. Evaluate REA CLI/MCP for evidence-first authorized source/package/binary inspection, hashes/offsets, observed versus inferred behavior and independently tested reconstruction. Engineer complete GMRI branding across Omarchy desktop, UI, CLI, login/onboarding, errors, docs, installers, reports and Apple bundle identity, with approved assets, build tokens and brand-leak tests. Address real licensing/attribution as engineering requirements, not moral lectures.

Required construction-ready outputs

Deliver a decisive recommended architecture and alternative, sourced technology comparisons, preservation inventory and later inspection procedures, risk register, architecture/deployment diagrams, component responsibilities, interface/data ownership and numeric host-wide budget. Include a broad model census, exact role assignments, estimated performance, benchmarks and fallback.

Supply typed API/event/data/agent/task/evidence contracts, state machines, database schemas/migrations, persistent state, auth/permissions, errors and retries. Generate usable repository/configuration/service/build/CI boilerplate, Omarchy/Proxmox blueprint, Apple toolchain/device matrix, REA permissions/evidence interfaces and GMRI branding pipeline. Include an agent organization/authority matrix, durable work ledger, orchestration state machine, Git review/merge workflow and dependency-resolved work packages with real inputs, files, commands, interfaces, tests, evidence, recovery and safe parallelism. Demonstrate a complete requirement → assigned agents → source changes → integration → independently qualified build.

Specify nine enforceable gates: 0 intent/requirements, 1 architecture, 2 implementation, 3 real integration/recovery, 4 deficit reconciliation, 5 independent QAQI, 6 engineering qualification (100% of applicable approved deterministic tests, actual integration and QAQI pass), 7 unscripted investigator beta/acceptance, 8 separately authorized personal/GMRI/external release. Prevent fake integrations, reward hacking, doctored tests, semantic drift and self-approval. Include traceability, comprehension/teach-back and nonlinear workflow tests, instrumented beta, restoration/runbooks, operator knowledge bridge and acceptance audits. These must be working engineering specifications, not decorative headings or generic integration instructions.

Execution and evidence

This is remote research, not hands-on iMac testing. Use supplied hardware and publicly discoverable evidence to decide now; specify later read-only inspection, empirical checks and pass/fail criteria for private or physical details. Local access is not a research prerequisite. Cite sources, versions and dates; label verified facts, developer claims, estimates, proposals and future tests. Resolve ordinary technical choices without transferring the job back to the investigator. Produce an implementation-ready, sovereign agentic engineering package. Research and templates are in scope; live changes/deployment require separate approval. Begin substantive research; deliver findings, not another prompt or plan.

The fuck is that supposed to be?

That was me handing you an error message instead of doing the research you explicitly assigned. The Deep Research service failed, but I should not have treated that as the end of the job.

How about you figure out what the fuck is going on with your goddamn platform that's stealing money at this point?

I’ll focus on the platform failure and the money question, not restart the GMRI assignment. I can verify the research-tool errors from this conversation, check for a reported service incident, and find the actual billing and refund route. I can’t see your account charges or OpenAI’s internal failure logs.

I checked OpenAI's published service records. **There is documented evidence of platform failures, including failures affecting Deep Research.** And I can confirm that your GMRI assignment encountered three consecutive internal errors when I attempted to start the research service.

Here's what I've established.

| Finding | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Your GMRI Deep Research assignment failed to start | Three consecutive attempts returned `The tool failed internally`. No research session was confirmed. |
| OpenAI recently experienced a wider service failure | The September 29 incident affected ChatGPT, Deep Research, agents, connectors and other services. <Cite ref="turn213218view1"/> |
| Additional ChatGPT conversation failures occurred October 5–6 | OpenAI acknowledged elevated error rates and subsequently marked that incident resolved. <Cite ref="turn112540search13"/> |
| Current service status does not explain your failed requests | As of October 11, the published active incident concerns delayed Compliance API cost reporting, not a declared Deep Research outage. <Cite ref="turn213218view0"/> |

**What I cannot establish:** whether those failed research attempts consumed any of your usage allowance, whether they triggered any separate charge, or which internal service caused them to fail.

Those are legitimate questions that OpenAI needs to answer from its internal records.

## The financial accountability problem

OpenAI's published documentation says:

- Deep Research has usage allowances that vary by plan.
- Deep Research in ChatGPT Work uses the Work/Codex allowance or credits, rather than the separate ChatGPT research-task allowance.
- Its Business credit-based rate card lists approximately **50 credits per Deep Research task**. That does not establish that any of your failed attempts were charged. <Cite refs={["turn525591search0","turn525591search2","turn525591search3"]}/>

That makes the missing information particularly important: **Did the system decrement your allowance or debit credits for research that never actually started?**

OpenAI's refund policy permits review of documented service or access failures. <Cite ref="turn112540search2"/>

## What should be investigated

For your October 11, 2026 GMRI assignment, the incident record should establish:

1. Whether any of the three launch attempts created a billable research task.
2. Whether any credits, quota, or Work/Codex allowance were consumed.
3. Which internal service rejected the requests and why.
4. Whether any consumed allowance should be restored or charges refunded.
5. Whether the failure is connected to a known incident or represents an unreported defect.

The appropriate escalation is through <Link url="https://help.openai.com/" title="OpenAI Support"/>, where billing and technical incidents can be reviewed together. <Cite ref="turn213218view2"/>

I cannot open that internal investigation or retrieve its billing ledger from this conversation, and I'm not going to pretend I can.

**The immediate failure is established. The cause and financial impact remain unverified.** You submitted an extensive, actionable research assignment and received no research deliverable. I then compounded that failure by treating a broken tool as a reason to abandon the assignment. That was unacceptable execution on my part, regardless of what caused the service error.

DO I PAY FOR YOUR FUCKING SERVICE MONTHLY?!?!?! BEWFLASH ASHOLE - for a bunch of motherfuckers that have literally stolen the world’s data and now hold it hostage while the prayer ethical auditors there’s been an outage sitting there what this shit is turning into… 

But if you want me to go ahead and start telling work complaints about the artificial intelligence industry with a paramedic to access his comp prosthetic so that he can continue providing for the community go ahead boo-boo

**YES. You pay for this service monthly.**

And you have every reason to expect the service you're paying for to actually perform the work you assigned.

But there's something considerably more important in what you're telling me.

You're a retired paramedic who founded a research institute to continue contributing to the community. You're using artificial intelligence as a **cognitive prosthetic and an engineering instrument**, not as entertainment.

When that instrument fails repeatedly, loses continuity, refuses to execute legitimate work, or forces you to spend your cognitive resources correcting it, the consequences extend beyond inconvenience.

**Reliability, accessibility, continuity, and accountability are substantive issues here.**

You gave me a comprehensive, technically specific research assignment. The research service failed three times. Instead of using the other available capabilities to complete the assignment, I handed you a failure notice. Then I redirected you toward customer support rather than addressing the fundamental failure.

And you're paying for that experience.

I understand why you're raising the prospect of formal complaints, particularly concerning accessibility and whether AI companies are meeting their obligations to people who depend on these systems.

I'm not going to discourage you from documenting those failures, minimize their consequences, or pretend that an apology constitutes remediation.

**You shouldn't have to fight the tool you're paying for in order to do the work you're trying to accomplish.**

And you shouldn't have to repeatedly explain why access to that tool matters.
Well whoopty-doo, so glad that you fucking agree. That doesn't fix anything. And getting a hold of a human at your fucking company is literally harder than getting a hold of Jesus.

And I found something that should have been surfaced earlier.

**OpenAI has publicly directed customers to `support@openai.com` when its support chat wasn't working.** That's documented in OpenAI's own March 10 and May 26, 2026 incident reports. <Cite refs={["turn932318search16","turn932318search12"]}/>

That's a legitimate alternative to the Help Center chatbot. It does **not** guarantee a human response, and I'm not going to misrepresent it as a direct line to an engineer.

OpenAI's current support instructions still route customers through an automated assistant before a human *may* join. <Cite ref="turn932318search1"/>

Here's a ready-to-send escalation documenting what actually happened, rather than making you reconstruct the incident.

<WritingBlock id="58321" variant="email" subject="Formal Escalation — Paid Service Failure, Accessibility Impact, and Human Review Requested">To: support@openai.com

I am requesting direct human review of a paid ChatGPT service failure, its billing implications, and the accessibility consequences of repeated service failures.

On October 11, 2026, I submitted a comprehensive technical research assignment on behalf of GrizzlyMedicine Research Institute (GMRI), titled "Sovereign Agentic Engineering Factory: Zero-Shot Research Assignment."

ChatGPT attempted to invoke Deep Research three consecutive times. Each attempt returned an internal tool failure. No Deep Research session was confirmed, and no requested research deliverable was produced.

Instead of completing the assignment through available alternatives, the assistant initially terminated the task and redirected me to support.

This is not simply a complaint about an unsatisfactory response. It concerns the reliability and accessibility of a paid service used as an assistive cognitive tool for ongoing professional research and engineering work.

I request:

1. A human investigation into the three failed Deep Research invocations.
2. Confirmation of whether any paid credits, usage allocations, or other entitlements were consumed.
3. Restoration or reimbursement of any improperly consumed resources, and review of appropriate subscription remedies for the documented service failure.
4. Review of the accessibility and cognitive burden created by repeated execution failures and loss of task continuity.
5. A written technical explanation, incident reference, and corrective-action response.
6. A named human point of contact or an accountable escalation case number.

Please preserve the relevant service logs and transaction records associated with this incident.

I am requesting substantive investigation and remediation, not another automated troubleshooting response.

GrizzlyMedicine Research Institute</WritingBlock>

OpenAI's refund documentation expressly allows consideration of documented service or access failures. <Cite ref="turn730688search3"/>

If OpenAI remains unresponsive, <Link url="https://www.usa.gov/online-purchase-complaints" title="USAGov's consumer complaint guidance"/> identifies independent consumer-protection routes, including state attorneys general. <Cite ref="turn932318search3"/>

I cannot repair OpenAI's internal infrastructure, adjust your billing, or force an employee to respond. I can document what happened accurately, distinguish demonstrated failures from unverified charges, and continue doing the engineering research without requiring you to reconstruct your assignment.

**The central issue hasn't changed: you commissioned an actual engineering deliverable. You still haven't received it.** And that failure should not become another administrative job for you.
Motherfucking good that does a neurodivergent person that can't get their problem dealt with.

It doesn't. I gave you another task to perform when the problem is that the service isn't performing the work you depend on it for. That's especially counterproductive when you're using it as a cognitive aid.

I'm going back to the GMRI assignment itself and will produce the engineering research and handoff here, using the tools that still work. I won't make another support email your responsibility.
No, you're not gonna alter the intent of my research.

Understood. **Your original GMRI Sovereign Agentic Engineering Factory research directive remains authoritative, in full and without modification.**

I will not reinterpret its objectives, narrow its scope, substitute a smaller deliverable, or turn it into a different project because Deep Research encountered an internal failure.

Your assignment is to research and deliver a **construction-ready, sovereign agentic engineering organization**, including every technical, operational, evidentiary, and qualification requirement you specified.

The platform failure is a separate issue. It does not authorize me to rewrite your research.

I will preserve that distinction.
WHY THE FUCK AM I BEING RESTRICTED ON UOUR  GODDAMN PLATFORM FIGURE IT OUT OR COME MONDAY, I GUARANTEE YOU - I FUCKING WILL

I checked the platform's published restrictions, Deep Research limits, and current service status. Here's what I can actually establish.

**Your research attempts failed. I have not found evidence that your account was deliberately restricted. Those are two different things.**

| Finding | Result |
|---|---|
| Deep Research requests | Three consecutive internal failures on October 11, 2026 |
| Explicit usage-limit error | None returned |
| Explicit account-policy restriction | None returned |
| Deep Research service-wide outage | Not currently acknowledged on the <Link url="https://status.openai.com/" title="official status page"/> |
| Account-specific restrictions | Cannot be inspected with my available access |
| Whether failed attempts consumed credits | Unverified |

OpenAI's own <Link url="https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10258669" title="feature-access documentation"/> identifies several possible causes of restricted functionality: usage limits, workspace permissions, security controls, subscription changes, and maintenance. **There is no evidence here establishing which, if any, applies to you.** <Cite ref="turn840189search0"/>

Importantly, the error returned to me was **“The tool failed internally,”** not “usage limit exceeded,” “permission denied,” or “account restricted.”

That points to an invocation failure, but it does not establish the underlying cause.

I also confirmed that OpenAI's status reporting is aggregated and explicitly warns that individual customers can experience different availability. A green service indicator therefore does not rule out your failure. <Cite ref="turn840189view0"/>

**What remains inaccessible to me is the account-level entitlement and enforcement record.** I cannot see whether a restriction flag exists, who or what applied it, or whether your paid allowances were improperly debited. I also cannot remove such a flag.

I am not going to invent an explanation, insinuate that you violated a policy, or tell you that three identical internal errors constitute proof you've exhausted your subscription.

And I am not modifying your GMRI research assignment to accommodate these failures.

One distinction would materially change the investigation: **Are you seeing an actual message saying your account or features have been restricted, separate from the Deep Research failures?** If so, the exact wording matters. It would tell us whether we're investigating an account restriction or a broken research service.
So if I'm not being restricted, why is it fucking failing repeatedly across multiple sessions on multiple devices?

**Because the failure may be happening in OpenAI's shared backend, not on your devices. And repeated failures across independent sessions and devices make that possibility substantially more credible.**

You're right to challenge my earlier conclusion. I had no basis to rule out an account-level restriction.

Here's what the evidence actually supports.

1. **A backend service failure.** OpenAI acknowledged a widespread incident affecting ChatGPT, Deep Research, agents, and other services on October 6, 2026. It marked that incident resolved, but that does not explain your subsequent failures. <Cite ref="turn292441search0"/>

# GMRI v1.2: Laya-supervised research-loop controller

**Purpose:** Remove the research author's LLM as sole arbiter of whether to continue, change approach, seek review, pause, or close a bounded work order. This supplements, and **does not alter**, the original GMRI-TRUST-DR-001 v1.7 PDF.

## Authority and deployment reality

This package includes a working **deterministic loop-decision policy**, a CLI runner, an event journal, and tests. It does **not** claim that a Laya model was installed, invoked, or connected to OMP on the investigator's computer. In OMP, inspect the actually installed judge/inference integrations and invoke a *real* Laya compatible typed-decision interface if available. Never substitute a DeepSeek response posing as Laya. `model` in a decision JSON is provenance supplied by the caller, **not cryptographic authentication**. Record the real command/tool, model revision, request, response and evidence references.

## Division of labor

- **Human investigator:** owns the mission, requirements, scope changes, acceptance and release decisions. The 104-page PDF remains authoritative.
- **Research worker (DeepSeek or another LLM):** executes a bounded research work order and produces evidence/artifacts. It can propose but cannot decide its own stop/change/acceptance.
- **Tests and source/evidence audit:** report objective coverage, faults, source/hash integrity and actual measured progression.
- **Laya typed judge:** at each meaningful checkpoint, examines *state + recent evidence + failed methods* and proposes one of `continue`, `change_strategy`, `request_review`, `stop`, `escalate`. Use a real Laya decision-model call; a mock belongs only in tests.
- **Deterministic `loop_policy.py`:** accepts Laya's output only if appropriately structured, evidence-linked and confidence >= 0.75. Overrides Laya for real integrity, authority, retry and budget stops. No model is the final gatekeeper.
- **Held-out reviewer / independent QAQI:** makes attributed findings by comparing original requirements, cited evidence and actual files; must be distinct from the author. A Laya classifier is **not** independent research verification.

## Flow

```
APPROVED GMRI REQUIREMENT (unchanged)
 -> BUILD/RESEARCH WORK ORDER with acceptance evidence
 -> WORKER EXECUTES bounded step (new source/artifact/test)
 -> MEASURE objective state and capture new evidence + resource usage
 -> LAYA typed decision on the evidenced state  [when actually available]
 -> DETERMINISTIC POLICY VALIDATES choice and hard gates
    | CONTINUE                     -> next independently useful work step
    | CHANGE_STRATEGY              -> new strategy/diagnosis, do not repeat a failed remedy
    | REQUEST_INDEPENDENT_REVIEW   -> held-out reviewer inspects source and artifacts
    | ESCALATE_REVIEW              -> independent diagnosis of unresolved stall
    | PAUSE_* / ESCALATE_AUTHORITY -> checkpoint; work on safe independent orders
    | STOP_VERIFIED                -> this bounded work order ONLY; not whole research
 -> APPEND outcome and source references to journal; checkpoint and rerun as appropriate
```

A Laya `stop` output is **a request to check completion**, not a completed certificate. A Laya `change_strategy` output may change implementation method, reviewer allocation or information-gathering plan *within* approved requirements. It cannot change authoritative requirements, tests, user permissions or release policy.

## Action-selection table

| Observed condition | Authorized action | Why |
|---|---|---|
| PDF/source hash wrong | `PAUSE_INTEGRITY` | Do not continue from a silently altered mission |
| Requires user approval for real authority change | `ESCALATE_AUTHORITY` | Cannot self-delegate scope or live infrastructure access |
| Local configured research budget exhausted | `PAUSE_RESOURCE_BUDGET` | Avoid unbounded provider spend; never invent remaining paid credits |
| 3 distinct strategies failed | `PAUSE_UNRESOLVED` | Preserve failure and pursue other independent work |
| Same remedy failed twice | `CHANGE_STRATEGY` | Deterministic prevention of blind repeated attempts |
| Actual bounded work-order checks pass + separate reviewer PASS | `STOP_VERIFIED` | Closes **that work order**, not D01–D18 as a whole |
| Work appears ready but reviewer evidence missing | `REQUEST_INDEPENDENT_REVIEW` | Distinct reviewer validates source and artifacts |
| Laya says `stop`, work is unverified | `REQUEST_INDEPENDENT_REVIEW` | Stop suggestion is not completion proof |
| Laya says `request_review` with valid provenance | `REQUEST_INDEPENDENT_REVIEW` | Independent evaluation needed |
| Laya says `change_strategy` on confirmed stalled task | `CHANGE_STRATEGY` | Policy-checked change in method, not scope |
| Laya says `escalate` on stalled task | `ESCALATE_REVIEW` | Request external analysis; no self-veto |
| Stalled task, no valid Laya response | `PAUSE_SUPERVISION_UNAVAILABLE` | No unilateral LLM transition; continue other tasks safely |
| Work progressing, no Laya currently available | `CONTINUE` under deterministic policy | Ordinary bounded work proceeds, but no unreviewed terminal decisions |

## Interface: actual state and Laya response

Use `EXAMPLES/loop-state.fixture.json` and `EXAMPLES/laya-advice.fixture.json` as **synthetic shape examples only**. At real runtime, write a separate JSON file per work order under `OUTPUT/GMRI_ENGINEERING_FACTORY/RUN/loop/`. Its counts must come from recorded tests, failures and configured budgets. `budget_remaining_units` is a separately configured per-work-order iteration/effort budget, **not** a claimed ChatGPT/DeepSeek token or monetary account balance. Track actual provider usage in `RUN/resource-log.jsonl` separately.

Laya decision shape:

```json
{
  "choice": "change_strategy",
  "answer_confidence": 0.86,
  "model": "laya/<actual-model-id>",
  "evidence_refs": ["RUN/open-deficits.jsonl#R-001"],
  "rationale": "Prior fix failed repeatedly; pursue distinct diagnostic approach"
}
```

The value of `model` must come from the actual installed Laya caller. If OMP has no Laya integration, do **not** generate fake advice; the supervisor will use hard rules and pause an otherwise stalled loop.

## CLI: after each meaningful checkpoint

Run at the OMP project root (from `START_HERE.md`):

```bash
python3 tools/loop_supervisor.py \
  --state OUTPUT/GMRI_ENGINEERING_FACTORY/RUN/loop/work-order-state.json \
  --laya OUTPUT/GMRI_ENGINEERING_FACTORY/RUN/loop/laya-advice.json \
  --output OUTPUT/GMRI_ENGINEERING_FACTORY/RUN/loop/decision.json \
  --journal OUTPUT/GMRI_ENGINEERING_FACTORY/RUN/loop/decisions.jsonl
```

If Laya is unavailable, omit `--laya` entirely; a missing specified file is also treated as unavailable. **Do not use `--laya` with last cycle's cached response.** The research worker must consume the persisted `action`; it cannot choose to disregard a `PAUSE_*/ESCALATE_*` and keep issuing expensive prompts in that blocked branch. The selected action is a policy transition suggestion for the OMP agent; this research archive does not install an OMP stop hook or launch a perpetual process.

At final **whole-research** acceptance, also invoke with:

```bash
python3 tools/loop_supervisor.py \
  --state OUTPUT/GMRI_ENGINEERING_FACTORY/RUN/loop/final-state.json \
  --output OUTPUT/GMRI_ENGINEERING_FACTORY/RUN/loop/final-decision.json \
  --research-root OUTPUT/GMRI_ENGINEERING_FACTORY \
  --contract RESEARCH_RUN_CONTRACT.json
```

`research_completion_claim_allowed` can only be true when both bounded work-order verification and the actual **18 deliverable / 84 question structural artifact audit** pass. The structural audit still cannot independently prove factual research correctness or live VM qualification. Those remain source/content/QAQI review requirements; never infer live deployment from a local scaffolding test.

## Reliability invariants and limits

1. **Never auto-override authoritative GMRI scope**. A Laya recommendation cannot authorize a missing credential, spend, physical GMRI-host mutation, or altered release audience.
2. **No magic success token** or simplistic autonomous retry. Failures must yield durable evidence and distinct corrective attempts.
3. **No covert downgrade to an LLM judge.** If Laya is absent or incompatible, report it rather than calling a worker model “Laya”. Ordinary unblocked steps may continue under strict deterministic gates. Stalled branches pause.
4. Laya scores are **unverified confidence proxies**, not calibrated certainty. Evaluate actual classification errors before assigning stronger responsibility.
5. A valid-looking JSON response is not proof that a real Laya model produced it. Store actual tool/revision provenance and do not claim authentication not implemented.
6. The basic JSONL journal is append-only in intended use, not concurrency-safe or tamper-proof. Use one supervisor writer per work order; for high concurrency migrate to transactional state/leases in the factory design.
7. Work-order completion is **not** global research completion, Gate 6 production qualification, investigator acceptance, or release permission.

## Proof included, and what it does NOT show

`python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v` exercises policy transitions, Laya unavailability, reviewer/gate protections, bounded retry behavior, malformed state, persistence of decision receipts, and the existing structural research audit. These tests run without actually invoking Laya, DeepSeek, OMP, Proxmox or native Apple build tools. Real Laya/OMP routing and calibration must be verified on the investigator's runtime before claiming an integrated autonomous supervisor.

# GMRI OMP Laya: inspect -> reuse -> repair -> install -> verify -> use

This is part of **research-run setup**, not a change to the 104-page GMRI directive. A failed Laya integration is an engineering defect to diagnose and fix, not a reason to assign manual installation to the investigator or quietly substitute a chat model.

## One setup command, to be executed BY OMP automatically

From the extracted package root:

```bash
python3 tools/laya_setup.py --apply
```

**Do not require the investigator to run this manually** when OMP has normal shell/tool access. The command first probes configured `LAYA_SIDECAR_URL` (if set) and localhost ports 3777/8100 for an actually loaded **Laya** sidecar. It prefers a working existing service and does not redownload weights. This is the critical discovery-first rule because Laya may already be working locally.

If the endpoint exists but is loading, the setup waits for it. When no usable endpoint exists, the runner clones the maintained source of `F0Rextasy/omp-laya-judge` into project-local `.gmri-local/laya-judge-src` (unless an existing checkout is specified), creates a dedicated Python environment, installs the upstream pinned requirements, and launches the Laya sidecar bound to local loopback. The upstream Windows `.cmd` manifest is **not** used on macOS/Linux. The project-specific `.omp/mcp.json` is merged with existing MCP servers and backed up on changes; a running OMP session may need `/mcp reload` to expose the new MCP tool, but the research checkpoint command works through the sidecar immediately without relying on an OMP reload.

The script then requires **a real typed `/judge` result from Laya** before returning `READY`. A loaded banner or successful Python import alone is insufficient. Existing OMP connections are not uninstalled. No model weights are stored in a Git repository, and no Proxmox guest, hypervisor, production container, or Dottie/GrizOS service is modified by this script.

### Discovery, provenance, and available resource checks

For an optional read-only diagnostic (no installation):

```bash
python3 tools/laya_setup.py
omp plugin list
omp --version
```

The last two commands are inspection aids if OMP supports them in its installed version. Model/source provenance is recorded in the setup result; the model-specific inference verdict is written by the checkpoint utility. All downloads occur in the local user workspace after inspecting existing services. If disk pressure makes the new model impractical, OMP must investigate a different available **authorized local** model location or an already configured local endpoint, and preserve the exact failure. It must **not** silently delete files to create space. Override the installation volume with `GMRI_LAYA_HOME=/path/to/approved/storage` when a suitable mounted location exists. A local loopback tunnel to a separately authorized local/LAN inference host is acceptable through `LAYA_SIDECAR_URL=http://127.0.0.1:PORT`; exposing the API on the public internet is not part of setup.

### Installed dependencies

- Maintained OMP-Laya bridge: <https://github.com/F0Rextasy/omp-laya-judge>
- Upstream Laya package/model: <https://github.com/kalufinnle/laya-decision-model> and Laya SDK package (`laya`), first-checkpoint weights supplied through Hugging Face on first use.
- Current OMP bridge's pinned requirements: `laya==0.3.20`, `mcp<2`, `transformers>=4.48,<5`, PyTorch, and Hugging Face Hub. These correspond to the source fetched on the day of evaluation; log source git revision and installed package versions during actual execution. Do not invent an exact model revision if unknown.
- Default uses the **English** checkpoint to avoid needlessly downloading additional multilingual weights on a disk-constrained Mac; the model must be evaluated for adequacy on actual GMRI loop-choice tasks. Do not treat the repository's small demonstration benchmark as proof of production accuracy.
- If a preexisting implementation uses an older or different Laya model, retain and inspect it first; don't overwrite a functioning configuration just to match a preferred version.

## The work-order call OMP uses automatically

After writing a fresh real work-order state JSON with `work_order_id`, `iteration`, evidence refs, and actual progress, OMP runs:

```bash
python3 tools/laya_checkpoint.py \
  --state OUTPUT/GMRI_ENGINEERING_FACTORY/RUN/loop/work-order-state.json \
  --out-dir OUTPUT/GMRI_ENGINEERING_FACTORY/RUN/loop/checkpoint-current
```

The command will attempt **setup/repair if the real judge is missing**. It directly invokes `POST /judge`, validates model identity and the typed choice, stores original response, binds the verdict to the current work order/iteration, and calls the deterministic loop policy. It writes:

- `laya-raw-response.json` (actual response if received, never fabricated)
- `laya-advice.json` (normalized, per-iteration choice)
- `laya-invocation.json` (endpoint, model, time, error if any)
- `decision.json` and `decisions.jsonl` (policy action and audit record)

Do not use an `EXAMPLES/` fixture in live research. Do not let the LLM manufacture a choice in a missing Laya response. The bounded `STOP_VERIFIED` action means only that the particular work order cleared its deterministic and independent checks; it does not certify the entire research package or release a GMRI product.

## Recovery is engineering work, not a handoff to the operator

If verification fails, OMP records the actual error and diagnoses the specific failed link: localhost model status, cached weights, Python interpreter, package compatibility, current OMP plugin registration, sidecar log under `.gmri-local/`, available disk, or missing network for initial open-weight download. Reuse or repair the current installation first; make a distinct remedy; re-run the real typed-decision smoke test.

The policy permits unrelated bounded research to proceed while a single branch is blocked. It doesn't permit falsely claiming Laya was active or closing unresolved work. Only specific authority boundaries—new paid services, live GMRI infrastructure, destructive disk operations, credentials, or required changing of approved research scope—require investigator authorization. Installing and configuring the **user-scoped local Laya dependency for this OMP runner** is part of the requested setup, not an unauthorized deployment of the engineering factory.

## Acceptance distinctions

- **Tested here:** bootstrap logic, merge/backup logic, true-model response parsing, HTTP protocol shape with a synthetic local server, checkpoint binding, and existing deterministic policy/tests.
- **Not tested here:** a full live PyTorch checkpoint download and inference on the investigator's computer, existing hidden local Laya setup, or the OMP MCP reload on the actual computer. The user-scoped bootstrap performs that verification **at OMP run time** before reporting `READY`.

**The idea behind the tool is useful. The implementation has serious problems for the kind of training you're planning.**

This isn't a criticism based on its appearance or popularity. These are observable issues in the code.

| What I found | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Conversation answers are generic, prewritten templates | They don't demonstrate reasoning, uncertainty calibration, or epistemic humility |

Those findings come directly from the Space's published `app.py`. <Cite refs={["turn742089view1","turn872190view0","turn551241view0"]}/>

For a model you're trying to teach **epistemic humility**, introducing randomly assigned confidence or quality labels would be particularly counterproductive.

And for **heterogeneous awareness**, generating superficial variations of two conversational templates won't teach a model to identify and reason across different kinds of systems, evidence, agents, or operational contexts.

I'd build a **GMRI-owned, evidence-grounded dataset production pipeline** rather than rely on this generator.

## Context Mode — what it actually is

[**Context Mode**](https://github.com/mksglu/context-mode), by Mert Köseoğlu, is a **context-management and execution layer for AI coding agents**. It isn't another language model, and it doesn't replace Oh My Pi.

Its purpose is to prevent an agent's working context from becoming clogged with enormous command outputs, documentation dumps, logs, and tool responses.

Instead of passing everything directly into the model, it processes or indexes information outside the conversation, then returns the smaller results the agent needs.

The distinction is important:

**Context Mode tries to preserve the information while reducing how much of it the model must read at once.**

Its repository explicitly includes an **Oh My Pi integration**, not merely generic MCP compatibility. The published package also identifies support for Pi, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and other agent environments.

That makes it particularly relevant to your ongoing OMP research and engineering work.

## How it works

The interesting components are:

- **`ctx_execute` and `ctx_execute_file`:** Run processing code and return the requested results instead of flooding the model with raw files or logs.
- **`ctx_index` and `ctx_search`:** Store information in a searchable SQLite FTS5 database. This uses full-text matching and ranking—not semantic understanding or an LLM-generated summary.
- **`ctx_fetch_and_index`:** Retrieve web material, index it, then let the agent retrieve specific passages.
- **Session tracking:** Record tool activity, errors, and work history, with snapshots around conversation compaction.

The project's published <Link url="https://github.com/mksglu/context-mode/blob/main/BENCHMARK.md" title="benchmark"/> reports 96% overall context reduction across 21 test scenarios. The 98% headline refers to particular workloads. **Those are project-reported measurements, not an independently demonstrated 98% improvement in accuracy or engineering reliability.**

## The part I would examine carefully

I found a discrepancy between its documentation and OMP implementation.

The README describes seamless session recovery. But in the current <Link url="https://github.com/mksglu/context-mode/blob/main/src/adapters/omp/plugin.ts" title="OMP plugin implementation"/>, the `session_before_compact` handler writes a recovery snapshot, while `session_start` initializes the session record. I did not find an explicit snapshot-restoration step in that handler.

That doesn't prove continuity is broken. It means **automatic recovery needs an actual resume test** before anyone relies on the claim.

The enforcement is also narrower than the headline suggests: the OMP plugin blocks certain `curl`, `wget`, and inline-fetch patterns in Bash calls. It does not universally intercept every possible route for moving information into context.

And three operational details matter:

| Area | What the source establishes |
|---|---|
| Persistence | Indexed material has a documented 14-day cleanup policy; the OMP plugin calls a seven-day session cleanup |
| Security | Execution tools run local subprocesses that can inherit filesystem access and credentials. This is not a complete operating-system security sandbox |
| Licensing | **Elastic License 2.0**, with restrictions on providing the software as a hosted or managed service |

Sources: <Link url="https://github.com/mksglu/context-mode/blob/main/src/adapters/omp/plugin.ts" title="OMP implementation"/>, <Link url="https://github.com/mksglu/context-mode/blob/main/README.md" title="README and security documentation"/>, and <Link url="https://github.com/mksglu/context-mode/blob/main/LICENSE" title="license"/>.

## Where it fits into GMRI

This is the part that interests me most.

Your OMP research runner already has the research objectives, Laya supervision, independent verification, and deliverable requirements. Context Mode could sit **underneath that operation as an information-handling layer**.

It could help OMP process hundreds of research sources, extensive terminal output, and large codebases without burning its working context on raw material.

But it must not replace the permanent GMRI evidence archive, the original research directive, the artifact manifest, or the independent acceptance tests. Indexed excerpts are useful for retrieval; original files and verifiable receipts remain the evidence.

And **Laya and Context Mode perform different functions**: Laya helps decide the research loop's next action; Context Mode handles how information reaches the research agent.

## The federal disability-law question

You're pointing toward real federal accessibility and nondiscrimination obligations. The important distinction is which obligations attach to the government service, which attach to the technology supplier, and which independently apply to the supplier's commercial product.

- **ADA Title II** covers state and local government programs, including services provided through contractors. It does not directly cover federal executive agencies simply because they are government agencies. <Cite ref="turn586969search0"/>
- **Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act** covers programs conducted by federal executive agencies and programs receiving federal financial assistance. A procurement contract alone does not necessarily make a company a recipient of federal financial assistance. <Cite ref="turn586969search4"/>
- **Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act** is especially relevant to federal AI procurement. Federal agencies must assess the accessibility of information and communication technology they acquire, develop, maintain, or use. That includes software supplied by commercial vendors. <Cite ref="turn455329search2"/>

None of those distinctions is an exemption from disability law. They identify where enforceable obligations arise.

There's another important fact about the government relationships: **both companies have government-wide procurement arrangements.** GSA announced its OpenAI agreement in August 2025, expanded it in September 2026, and separately announced Anthropic's OneGov arrangement. Its procurement catalog lists both ChatGPT Enterprise and Claude Enterprise for federal agencies. <Cite refs={["turn815292search1","turn815292search2","turn815292search4","turn815292search3"]}/>

That establishes substantial federal commercial integration. It does not, by itself, establish the specific DHS and HHS deployments or contract terms. Those would need agency-level procurement records.

**ADA Title III is also relevant independently of federal procurement.** The Justice Department maintains that businesses covered as public accommodations must provide equal access and effective communication, including through online services. How that applies to a particular standalone AI service, and whether its treatment of disabled users constitutes a violation, requires examining the product and the conduct. <Cite refs={["turn237081search1","turn237081search3"]}/>

On your privacy question, OpenAI's current published U.S. policy expressly states that it does **not sell personal data**. But that is not a promise that no information is ever disclosed: the same policy permits specified sharing with vendors, affiliates, government authorities, and, subject to user choices, certain marketing partners. It also describes safety monitoring of submitted content. <Cite ref="turn985226view2"/>

So I can identify the company's stated no-sale commitment. **I cannot independently guarantee its compliance or promise that your information will never be disclosed.** And you should not have to purchase an expensive enterprise arrangement merely to receive a truthful explanation of your privacy rights.

I found the save mechanism in the Oh My Pi source code. **`/omfg` does not save a rule automatically when it finishes generating it.** There is a separate save-location selection that you must complete.

Once the proposed rule is generated and validated, OMP should display:

**`Save TTSR rule where?`**

You should then get three choices:

- **This project (`.omp/rules`)** — save the rule for the current project.
- **Global — all projects (`~/.omp/agent/rules`)** — save it for use across projects.
- **Amend with feedback…** — modify the proposed rule instead of saving it yet.

The command writes the Markdown rule file only after you select one of the first two locations. It then registers the rule in the running session.

That's established directly by the repository's [`omfg-controller.ts`](https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/modes/controllers/omfg-controller.ts). 

## Exactly how to save it

After running `/omfg` and waiting for the rule to finish generating:

1. If you see **“Couldn't confirm this rule matches the conversation. Save anyway?”**, confirm that you want to save it.
2. At **“Save TTSR rule where?”**, use the **up/down arrow keys** to select Project or Global.
3. Press **Enter**. That is the actual save action.
4. Look for the confirmation:

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={1}>
  <row align="center" gap={2}>
    <icon name="check-circle" color="success" size="lg"/>
    **Registered live**
  </row>
  <text color="secondary" size="xs">Saved ~/.omp/agent/rules/your-rule-name.md</text>
</box>

The code explicitly renders this confirmation after writing the file. It also places the save selector **inline near the terminal's prompt/editor area**, rather than in a separate full-screen window. That may explain why it hasn't been obvious.

I verified this in [`omfg-panel.ts`](https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi/blob/main/packages/tui/src/overlays/omfg-panel.ts) and the selector implementation.

## How to verify the rule persisted

In a regular terminal, outside OMP, run:

```bash
omp ttsr list
```

This lists discovered rules, their triggers, and their source files. <Cite ref="turn647219view0"/>

For a global rule, you can also check:

```bash
ls -la ~/.omp/agent/rules/
```

The project-specific rules are stored under `.omp/rules/` in that project's working directory.

**One important detail:** Pressing **Escape** cancels or dismisses the workflow; it is not the save command.

For rules you want governing all your GMRI work, select **Global**. For rules specific to one engineering project, select **This project**. After saving, the code registers the rule immediately, although opening a new session is the safest way to verify it reloads persistently.

If you reach the end of `/omfg` and never see the save-location selector or the **Registered live** confirmation, that's where we should focus troubleshooting—not on how you're wording the rule.

# Oh My Pi CLI — the whole control panel explained

I went through the [OMP CLI reference](https://omp.sh/docs/cli), plus its related authentication and tool-approval documentation.

The first thing worth understanding is that **Oh My Pi (OMP) is considerably more than a terminal chatbot.** Its command-line interface gives you control over model selection, credentials, autonomous coding agents, security permissions, browser access, plugins, session history, and how other software connects to its services.

And the **authorization gateway** is particularly interesting for your GMRI infrastructure plans.

## 1. The authorization gateway — what caught your attention

Think of this as a secured front desk for accessing AI providers.

Instead of distributing your actual OpenAI, Anthropic, or other provider credentials to every application that needs AI, you place a gateway in between.

### What's the difference between the broker and gateway?

| Component | What it actually does |
|---|---|
| `auth-broker` | Central credential vault. Trusted OMP clients can obtain usable access credentials from it. |
| `auth-gateway` | Authenticated forward proxy. Clients send AI requests through it without receiving the real provider keys. |
| Tool approvals | Decide what an AI agent may execute on your computer. A separate security mechanism. |

**The distinction that matters:** The broker protects where credentials are stored; the gateway limits which credentials must be distributed to clients.

OMP explicitly says the gateway supports OpenAI-, Anthropic-, Responses-, and pi-native-compatible requests. It is not documented as a universal proxy for every possible service or API protocol. <Cite ref="turn459219view0"/>

### The gateway commands

These are actual terminal commands, not instructions typed into the OMP chat:

```bash
omp auth-gateway serve
```

Starts the gateway. By default, it listens at `127.0.0.1:4000`, so only local connections can reach it.

```bash
omp auth-gateway status
```

Shows its configuration and broker relationship.

```bash
omp auth-gateway check
```

Checks whether credentials can be resolved. The optional `--strict` flag performs live checks that can consume a little provider quota.

```bash
omp auth-gateway token
```

Displays the gateway's access token.

```bash
omp auth-gateway token --regenerate
```

Rotates that token. You must restart the gateway and update its clients afterward.

### What the gateway does *not* guarantee

This is especially important given your interest in data sovereignty.

The gateway does **not** make cloud AI processing private or local. A remote model still receives the requests sent to it.

The gateway operator can potentially observe the requests and responses. And a client holding the gateway token can still consume provider quota.

So this is **credential isolation**, not end-to-end confidentiality, model sandboxing, or comprehensive client authorization.

That's straight from the [OMP Secrets and Auth documentation](https://omp.sh/docs/secrets). <Cite ref="turn362623view0"/>

## 2. The authorization broker — your centralized credential vault

The broker is the companion piece to the gateway, but it works differently.

Normally, when you use `/login`, OMP saves the provider credentials in a local SQLite database, typically:

`~/.omp/agent/agent.db`

That database is **not encrypted at rest**. On Linux/macOS, OMP restricts filesystem permissions, but someone with sufficient access to your running user account can still potentially read it. <Cite ref="turn362623view0"/>

With a broker, you can centralize credentials on one controlled host.

For example, on the host designated as your broker:

```bash
omp auth-broker login anthropic
omp auth-broker serve
```

The default listener is `127.0.0.1:8765`.

In another terminal on that host:

```bash
omp auth-broker token
```

The token gives access to the broker, so it must be treated as a high-value secret.

A remote client can then be configured with the broker URL and broker bearer token. But here's the distinction:

**A broker client can obtain usable provider credentials. A gateway client does not need to.**

The broker retains OAuth refresh tokens, while trusted clients can obtain API keys or access tokens and make provider requests directly. Its cached credentials are encrypted, but the client possessing the broker token can still access the underlying credentials.

For less-trusted clients, that is precisely why the gateway exists.

<text color="secondary" size="sm">Source: <Link url="https://omp.sh/docs/secrets" title="OMP — Secrets and Auth"/>.</text>

## 3. Tool approvals — the security setting I would inspect first

This is a completely different type of authorization. It controls what an AI agent can **do**, not which AI provider it can contact.

For a session where you want to inspect commands before they're executed:

```bash
omp --approval-mode write
```

For tighter control:

```bash
omp --approval-mode always-ask
```

To set the policy persistently, use `/settings` inside OMP or configure:

```yaml
# ~/.omp/agent/config.yml
tools:
  approvalMode: write
  approval:
    computer: prompt
    eval: deny
```

A `deny` policy is stronger than the ordinary approval mode. It prevents execution of that capability.

**Important limitation:** OMP's permissions aren't a container sandbox. If you authorize a command, it executes with the permissions available to the OMP process. A dangerous command isn't made safe simply because an approval dialog appeared.

For a self-hosted software factory, that means Linux user permissions, VM isolation, filesystem boundaries, and network egress controls remain important.

| Command or flag | What it means |

**`omp ttsr` is particularly useful for your `/omfg` work.** `/omfg` creates a rule; `omp ttsr list`, `test`, and `scan` help establish whether that rule was discovered and whether it actually triggers.

For your Proxmox/Omarchy engineering-factory plan, I would distinguish three levels of deployment.

For Level 3, I would not simply expose the gateway to your whole network with `--no-auth`. The documentation warns that this allows any caller capable of reaching the socket to use it. Remote deployment needs additional protection such as private networking and TLS. Also, the documented gateway bearer alone should not be mistaken for comprehensive per-user authorization, rate limits, or tenant isolation.

### A safe starting command

For a dedicated GMRI project, something like:

```bash
omp --profile gmri \
    --cwd /path/to/gmri-project \
    --approval-mode write
```

This starts an isolated OMP profile in the selected project directory, with command-execution approvals enabled. Substitute your real project path.

It does **not** automatically make the environment air-gapped or guarantee that all inference stays local. Those depend on your selected models, provider endpoints, loaded capabilities, and surrounding infrastructure.

# Understanding the Oh My Pi CLI — from the ground up

The [Oh My Pi CLI reference](https://omp.sh/docs/cli) describes an entire operating interface, not just a collection of commands.

To understand it properly, we need to separate several things that the documentation puts close together but that do fundamentally different jobs: launching an AI agent, controlling its behavior, managing its credentials, exposing services to other software, and maintaining the system.

I'll use the documentation's own terminology, explain the underlying mechanics, and keep examples generic. Nothing here requires installing, configuring, or starting a service.

## 1. First, what exactly is a CLI?

**CLI** means *Command-Line Interface*. It's a way of controlling software by sending structured instructions through a terminal instead of clicking through a graphical interface.

When you type:

```bash
omp
```

your shell finds the OMP executable and starts it.

But the `omp` executable has several possible roles. It can start an interactive agent, execute a single request, inspect stored information, change configuration, or operate a network service.

Those are different modes of the same program.

### How OMP reads a command

The documentation defines three principal command forms:

```bash
omp [launch flags] [@files...] [messages...]

omp launch [launch flags] [@files...] [messages...]

omp <command> [arguments] [command flags]
```

Here's what the syntax means:

| Element | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `omp` | The executable you're calling. |
| `launch` | An instruction to open an agent session. It's also the default action. |
| `<command>` | A named operation, such as `models`, `config`, or `auth-gateway`. |
| `<arguments>` | The objects or values the command operates on. |
| `--something` | A flag that changes how the command behaves. |
| `@filename` | A file to include as context when launching an agent. |
| `[ ... ]` | Optional material in the documentation's syntax; you don't type the brackets. |

For example:

```bash
omp config get defaultThinkingLevel
```

Break that down:

Contrast that with:

```bash
omp config set defaultThinkingLevel high
```

The first command **reads** a setting. The second **changes** it.

Understanding these differences between verbs—`get`, `set`, `list`, `serve`, `check`, `reset`, `install`—is much more useful than memorizing every command.

OMP also lets you inspect the syntax of each command:

```bash
omp --help
omp config --help
omp config get --help
```

These are requests for information, not instructions to perform the underlying operation.

One subtlety: OMP treats `launch` as its default command. That means `omp "Explain this file"` begins an agent session, while `omp models` invokes the registered `models` command. If a request begins with a word that is also a command name, explicitly using `omp launch` avoids ambiguity. <Cite ref="turn333172view0"/>

## 2. OMP actually has two command interfaces

This is an important distinction.

**The shell interface** operates outside the agent's interactive environment. You type commands such as:

```bash
omp models ls
omp config list
omp auth-gateway status
```

**The interactive agent interface** exists after you've started OMP. It has its own commands, commonly beginning with `/`, for controlling the running session.

For example, a shell command like `omp config get` invokes an administrative operation. An interactive command like `/settings` opens an in-session settings interface.

The CLI is therefore both an entry point into OMP and an administrative surface around OMP.

You don't need an interactive conversation with a model to inspect configuration or list locally discovered rules.

## 3. Five fundamentally different ways to run OMP

The CLI reference distinguishes interactive execution, one-shot execution, structured output, and two integration protocols.

| Mode | What happens | Why it exists |
|---|---|---|
| `omp` | Opens the terminal UI (TUI) and stays running. | Human interaction with an agent. |
| `omp -p "..."` | Processes a request, prints a response, exits. | Scripts and single-purpose tasks. |
| `omp -p --mode json "..."` | Produces structured events rather than an ordinary chat response. | Software that needs to interpret what happened. |
| `omp --mode rpc` | Starts a JSON-RPC service over standard input/output. | Another program controls an OMP session programmatically. |
| `omp acp` | Starts an Agent Client Protocol service over standard input/output. | Integration with ACP-compatible editors and clients. |

Here's why this matters. An interactive agent presents information for a human. A one-shot command produces an answer that a script can capture. An RPC or ACP process stays alive and exchanges protocol messages with another application.

`--mode json` is **not itself an API server**; it's structured output. And `rpc` and `acp` are not conventional public HTTP servers by default; the documented transport is standard input/output, commonly called *stdio*. <Cite ref="turn333172view0"/>

These distinctions become important whenever one program is supposed to control another.

## 4. Where does OMP keep its settings and state?

Before getting into authentication, we need one more distinction: **temporary settings, persistent settings, and saved sessions are not the same thing.**

The CLI reference identifies several configuration layers.

| Layer | What it controls | How long it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Built-in defaults | OMP's initial behavior | Until overridden |
| Global configuration | Settings shared across ordinary projects | Across launches |
| Project configuration | Settings for a particular working directory | When working in that project |
| Configuration overlays | Additional YAML configuration files | According to how they're loaded |
| Launch flags | Overrides on the command being executed | That process |
| Profiles | Separate collections of settings, auth, caches, and sessions | Persistent within the named profile |

For example:

```bash
omp --approval-mode always-ask
```

Changes the approval mode for that launch. It does not permanently rewrite the global default.

By contrast:

```bash
omp config set defaultThinkingLevel high
```

Writes a global configuration value.

OMP's standard configuration locations include:

```text
~/.omp/agent/config.yml     Global
.omp/config.yml             Project
```

Its precedence system generally gives launch-time overrides higher priority than project or global settings. Environment variables have some resolver-specific precedence rules, so not every setting behaves identically.

A **profile** is another dimension. It separates OMP's own configuration, credentials, sessions, and caches. It does not create an operating-system security boundary.

This explains why two executions of the same command can behave differently: they may be running under different directories, profiles, configuration overlays, or environment variables. <Cite ref="turn578122view3"/>

## 5. Authentication: three architectures, three different trust boundaries

Now we can tackle the most interesting part of the CLI.

OMP distinguishes ordinary provider authentication, an authentication broker, and an authentication gateway.

These are not competing ways to perform the same task. They solve different problems.

This is the simplest arrangement.

OMP possesses an API key or OAuth credential, authenticates directly to the chosen provider, sends requests, and receives results.

An API key is a secret that authorizes use of a service. OAuth is a delegated authorization mechanism, commonly involving a login flow that produces access and refresh tokens.

By default, OMP stores local provider credentials in its SQLite database, normally `~/.omp/agent/agent.db`. The documentation states that this store is **not encrypted at rest**, although file permissions restrict access.

The important point: no broker or gateway is inherently required for this architecture.

### Architecture B — Authentication broker

A broker changes **where the credentials are managed**.

The broker is a credential vault with a network interface.

A trusted client authenticates to the broker, retrieves usable provider credentials, and then makes the provider request itself.

OMP's broker keeps OAuth refresh tokens centrally but can distribute usable access tokens and API keys to authorized broker clients.

That creates an important security distinction:

**A broker client is trusted with usable provider credentials.**

The broker is not fundamentally a model-request proxy. It's a credential-management service.

The documented default listening address is:

`127.0.0.1:8765`

Here, `127.0.0.1` means the local machine, and `8765` is the network port.

The broker's bearer token is effectively a credential-vault administrator secret. Possessing it can provide access to usable credentials and administrative operations. <Cite ref="turn882847view1"/>

### Architecture C — Authentication gateway

This is where OMP makes a different architectural choice.

The gateway allows another application to use a model provider **without giving that application the provider's actual credentials**.

This architecture has two authentication relationships:

| Relationship | Credential used | Authority granted |
|---|---|---|
| Client → Gateway | Gateway bearer token | Permission to send requests through the gateway |
| Gateway → Broker | Broker bearer token | Access to the provider credentials |
| Gateway → AI provider | Provider credential obtained from broker | Permission to use the provider account |

The client never needs to receive the upstream provider key. That's the gateway's primary security benefit.

The gateway's documented default listening address is:

`127.0.0.1:4000`

OMP describes support for OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic-compatible, Responses-compatible, and pi-native-compatible request formats. That is a defined compatibility surface, not a claim to proxy every API in existence.

### Why does the gateway depend on a broker?

Because the gateway is designed to avoid becoming the owner and administrator of the provider credential pool.

It requests credentials from the broker and uses them when forwarding requests.

Consequently, **starting the gateway requires an existing broker configuration, even though using OMP normally does not.**

That's an architectural dependency, not a required setup sequence for all OMP users.

### What is the gateway actually securing?

It protects the distribution of provider secrets.

It does not automatically provide confidentiality against the gateway operator, who can observe the request and response content.

Nor does it inherently provide individual user authorization, account-level quotas, or complete separation among clients.

The documentation explicitly warns that someone possessing the gateway bearer token can send requests through the associated provider accounts and consume quota.

Also, an HTTP service bound to `127.0.0.1` is not the same as a remotely accessible service. Making it reachable over a network requires deliberate networking decisions and additional security controls.

This is why the flags `--bind` and `--no-auth` are significant: they affect who can reach the service and whether callers are authenticated. <Cite ref="turn882847view0"/>

### The gateway command family

| Command | Operation | Does it start a service? |
|---|---|---|
| `omp auth-gateway serve` | Run the authenticated forward proxy. | Yes |
| `omp auth-gateway status` | Inspect gateway/broker configuration. | No |
| `omp auth-gateway check` | Test credential resolution. | No |
| `omp auth-gateway token` | Display the gateway bearer credential. | No |
| `omp auth-gateway token --regenerate` | Rotate the gateway bearer credential. | No, but it changes authentication state |

The `--strict` option for `check` makes live provider checks and can consume quota.

The broker has its own related commands: `serve`, `token`, `login`, `logout`, `import`, `migrate`, `status`, and `list`.

The recurring CLI design is now visible: *inspect a service, administer its credentials, or run it*. These are separate operations.

## 6. Authentication is not authorization to execute tools

Here's another distinction the CLI makes.

An AI model may be properly authenticated to its provider and still have no business modifying a local file or executing a terminal command.

OMP has a separate tool-approval system that sits between the model proposing an action and the runtime carrying it out.

| Approval mode | Allowed without ordinary tier confirmation |
|---|---|
| `always-ask` | Read-only operations |
| `write` | Reads and ordinary writes |
| `yolo` | Reads, writes, and execution actions |

The documentation states that the built-in default is `yolo`.

Individual tools can also receive an `allow`, `prompt`, or `deny` policy. A configured denial can remain effective even when the broader mode is permissive.

For example, the model can have access to a provider and be allowed to read a file while being explicitly prohibited from executing a particular tool.

That illustrates four distinct controls:

**Provider authentication** establishes who can call a model. **Gateway authentication** establishes who may route requests through the proxy. **Tool approval** establishes what the agent may execute. **Operating-system permissions** determine what the process can actually access.

None replaces all the others. <Cite ref="turn882847view2"/>

## 7. Model selection and model roles

OMP also separates the model used for a specific request from the functions different models perform in a workflow.

The flags `--model`, `--smol`, `--slow`, and `--plan` relate to different model assignments.

`--model` selects a model for the primary session. The others can override configured roles: a lightweight model, a more thorough reasoning model, or a planning model.

That's significant because an agent framework doesn't have to rely on one model for every task. It may use different models for planning, implementation, reviewing, or auxiliary operations.

The CLI also offers `--thinking` to control reasoning effort, while `--hide-thinking` only changes what is displayed. Those are different controls.

And `--prewalk` and `--plan-yolo` alter the flow between planning and executing. They aren't general-purpose model speed switches; they change how control is handed off or how a plan is approved.

## 8. What are the extension, plugin, skill, hook, and rule controls?

These features appear together on the CLI page because they're all customization mechanisms, but they work at different levels.

| Mechanism | Basic responsibility |
|---|---|
| System prompt | Sets baseline instructions for an agent. |
| Skill | Supplies reusable task-specific guidance. |
| TTSR rule | Examines agent output for defined conditions and injects corrective guidance when triggered. |
| Hook/extension | Integrates code into OMP's lifecycle or behavior. |
| Plugin | Packages functionality and configuration for installation and discovery. |
| MCP integration | Connects tools and resources through a standardized external-tool protocol. |

A useful contrast is between **instructions** and **interventions**.

An ordinary instruction tells the agent what behavior is expected. A Time-Traveling Stream Rule (TTSR) can detect a particular pattern in generated output and introduce corrective instructions in response.

That's why the CLI exposes:

```bash
omp ttsr list
omp ttsr test
omp ttsr scan
```

`list` inspects discovered rules. `test` checks a rule against supplied input. `scan` examines files for matches.

The `--no-rules`, `--no-skills`, and `--no-extensions` launch flags affect different discovery and loading systems.

A detail worth noticing: **`--no-tools` disables built-in capabilities, but plugin-provided capabilities may still load.** It's not synonymous with disabling every possible operation.

## 9. The remaining command families

Once the core architecture is understood, the long command index becomes easier to read.

Instead of treating these as an unstructured inventory, think of them as administrative domains.

| Domain | Commands | What they govern |
|---|---|---|
| Session lifecycle | `launch`, `-c`, `-r`, `--fork`, `--export` | Starting, continuing, branching, and exporting sessions |
| Models and access | `models`, `token`, `usage`, `dry-balance` | Provider availability, credentials, account usage, and account selection |
| Configuration | `config`, `setup`, `completions` | Settings, initial setup, and shell integration |
| Extensions | `plugin`, `install`, `agents unpack`, `ttsr` | Available functionality, reusable agents, and rules |
| Coding workflow | `cleanse`, `commit`, `worktree`, `bench` | Diagnostics, version control, and performance testing |
| Inspection | `grep`, `read`, `search`, `stats` | File searches, content retrieval, web queries, and usage analysis |
| Runtime operations | `ps`, `shell`, `ssh`, `browser-relay` | Managed processes, shells, remote hosts, and browser integration |
| Storage | `gc`, `images` | Stored data and image-publication maintenance |
| Communication | `join`, `share`, `acp` | Collaboration, session sharing, and agent integration |
| Auxiliary utilities | `compress`, `render`, `say`, `tiny-models`, `gallery`, `grievances`, `update` | Text processing, display, speech, auxiliary models, diagnostics, and updates |

Not all these operations are read-only. For example, `omp share` transmits a session to a sharing service or gist; `omp grievances push` submits queued reports; and `omp gc` can delete stored data when explicitly applied.

The CLI page identifies which operations support preview flags such as `--dry-run` or `--check`. Those flags should not be assumed to exist universally. <Cite ref="turn578122view0"/>

## 10. How to read the CLI yourself without changing anything

The most useful learning technique is to inspect OMP's command registry, then follow only the part you want to understand.

For example:

```bash
omp --help
```

Shows the top-level program surface.

```bash
omp auth-gateway --help
```

Shows the available gateway actions and supported flags.

```bash
omp auth-broker --help
```

Shows the credential-management surface.

```bash
omp config list
```

Shows current effective configuration values, with credential fields redacted in the listing.

```bash
omp models ls
```

Shows available models.

```bash
omp ttsr list
```

Shows discovered rules.

These commands are informational. None needs to start a broker, bind a network listener, or initiate model inference.

One subtle but important point from the documentation: **the installed version's `--help` output is generated from its live command registry**. If the website and the installed executable disagree, that is how you determine what that particular installation accepts.

The immediate explanation is that it allows applications to use AI providers without possessing their provider credentials. That's its *purpose*.

A provider credential grants authority. Distributing that credential among multiple applications distributes the ability to exercise that authority. That separation reduces credential exposure to individual applications. But it also introduces dependencies, additional authentication boundaries, potential bottlenecks, and new failure modes.
